prize_parts.citation: For a body of large, polyphonic novels and related prose that remakes the English-language novel through Indigenous oral storytelling, mythic register and ecological time.

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged: Wright alone. The reason is not that I have found a decisive new argument. After the exchange, the question the chair asked me is the one that matters, so I try to answer it. As publicly known, Carpentaria and The Swan Book are followed by the very long novel Praiseworthy, and there is also earlier and parallel work, including a first novel, nonfiction and the collective memoir Tracker. If Praiseworthy extends the polyphonic, mythic and satirical method into a new situation rather than restating it, then the oeuvre spans roughly three decades and several books, and the durability worry is weaker than a count of two major novels suggests. I cannot verify this. It remains a premise I hold from public knowledge and not a finding. The core of the case is still prose and structure: a narrative voice that takes its architecture, its time and its collective speaking from Aboriginal oral practice, and that holds sovereignty, memory and environmental catastrophe in one language. I read that as a formal departure inside English and not as a theme. My preference over Cărtărescu and Michon is a close judgment of degree. Palm's and Sem-Sandberg's exchange has made me more confident that Cărtărescu is a real contender, and I name him as my first alternative.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is still the base for a whole-oeuvre citation. If Praiseworthy does not sustain the standard of Carpentaria, or if the later work merely enlarges it, the case thins to two books. A second reservation is that the committee can assess Wright's idiom and oral rhythm only from outside, and a reader outside that context may overrate or underrate it. A third is that the cultural and political stakes of the work are visible and easy to cite, and they could carry the argument when the prose should. I have no better answer to the third than to insist that the argument be made on sentences and structure. Cărtărescu offers a longer record and Michon a tighter one, and either could reasonably be judged to meet 'sustained quality' more clearly than Wright.

responses.point: Olsson asks for specific evidence on what Adonis's poems do at the level of the line, kept separate from reception and the essays, and for explicit examination of the later volumes against the early landmarks. He also says he places Wright sixth because durability is untested and he wants to see what followed the two major novels.
responses.response: Your question about what followed the two major novels is fair, and I answer it only partly: I know of Praiseworthy and the nonfiction, but I cannot verify them, so my case should not be treated as mature on my word alone. I would apply the same discipline to Adonis. If the committee obtains expert assessment of the Arabic originals, and it shows that the poems carry the argument without leaning on influence or the essays, that would change what I can say about him. At present I cannot judge the line and so cannot rank him above a candidate whose formal departure I can follow in English. I do not read that as a verdict against him. It is a limit on what I can honestly claim, and I think you accept that limit too.

responses.point: Mattson, who keeps Michon first, says breadth is not volume and that the same questions about vocation, anonymity and the afterlife of lives are pursued with increasing exactness. She also asks the committee to confirm that Michon's later books keep the standard of Small Lives and The Eleven, and in her response to me says she cannot judge whether Wright's achievement is repeated or concentrated in two books.
responses.response: I accept the distinction between breadth and volume, and it applies to me as much as to you. My answer to your doubt about Wright is that the later work, as I know it publicly, appears to enlarge the earlier method into new subject matter, but I have flagged that I cannot verify this, and that is exactly the test you propose for Michon. We ask the same question of both of us, and neither of us has an answer from evidence supplied here. I also take your point that translation risk should not fall only on the writer with compressed prose: Wright's English is exposed to a different loss, the oral register that a reader outside the tradition may not hear. Where I still differ is on range. Michon's method is deliberately single, and I think Wright's polyphony, which moves between many voices and registers, gives a wider formal range even in a smaller number of books. I do not claim that is settled.

responses.point: Palm ranks Cărtărescu first and says the late large works enlarge rather than restate the earlier world. She suggests a fair test is whether the committee can name what changes between Blinding and Solenoid. She also keeps Wright as her second alternative and says her hesitation about Wright is the modest fiction corpus and the partly legible relation of the English to Indigenous traditions.
responses.response: Your test is the right one and I would turn it on my own candidate: what changes between Carpentaria and The Swan Book, and then in Praiseworthy? From public knowledge, the first is anchored in a specific northern place and community, the second moves toward a dystopian near-future, and the later novel again changes the scale. That suggests development and not restatement, but I hold it provisionally. I agree that your argument about extension answers the repetition worry better than the objections raised against Cărtărescu so far. That is why he is my first alternative. Where I still prefer Wright is that her form draws on a living collective oral practice and not on a single author's cosmology. I accept that this is an argument about significance and could be weighed the other way, and I would not want to claim it as a finding about merit.

responses.point: Swärd keeps Cărtărescu first and Wright as first alternative. She says the gap is narrow and turns on whether depth in a few very large novels outweighs a longer body of work, and she suggests the architecture of long novels may survive translation better than prosody.
responses.response: I agree that the gap is narrow and that it turns on depth against breadth. Your suggestion that architecture survives translation better than prosody is plausible and I cannot test it. It cuts in a way I find useful for Wright as well: the polyphonic structure, the handling of time and the collective voice are architectural, so they may travel better than her sentence-level idiom. If that is right, translation risk is not a common discount but varies with where each writer's achievement sits, and the committee should say so openly. I would still not rely on this to choose between us. I hold it as a hypothesis.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg ranks Michon first and Wright second. He says two major novels, with nonfiction and a later novel he knows less well, make a thinner base for a whole-oeuvre citation than the one he proposes for Michon, though the difficulty is of the same kind. He also insists that Wright's case must rest on prose and structure and not on the political significance of the subject.
responses.response: I accept the standard you set, and I think the committee should hold both of us to it. I would add that the difficulty is not entirely of the same kind. Michon's consistency across a compact corpus is a form of sustained quality that is easy to state, whereas mine depends on reading a smaller number of very large books as sustained. I agree that this makes the base thinner for a whole-oeuvre citation, and it is the main reason my preference for Wright is provisional. Your distinction between sustained quality and significance is useful. Michon seems to me to meet the first very clearly and the second less clearly. For Wright I would reverse the emphasis, and I would want the committee to argue that on specific passages.

uncertainties: I have not independently verified any text. My knowledge of Praiseworthy, the nonfiction and Tracker is public and thinner than my knowledge of Carpentaria and The Swan Book, so the claim of continued development is unverified.
How much a small number of very large novels weighs against sustained quality across a whole oeuvre is unresolved, and it depends partly on whether the later work extends or restates the earlier.

Wright's English is shaped by Indigenous idiom and oral rhythm, and the committee's ability to judge it from outside that context is uncertain. Whether architecture travels better in translation than sentence-level idiom is a hypothesis I cannot test.

For Cărtărescu and Michon, the fidelity of translation of dense Romanian and French prose is unknown, and for Adonis the achievement lies in Arabic prosody that I cannot assess directly. All comparisons with Wright remain provisional.
Whether a co-opted member votes in committee is undocumented. My simulated vote is a modeling assumption.
statement.conflict_note: No connection to any shortlisted writer is recorded in the supplied profile. As Permanent Secretary and a co-opted member, I hold a role in the committee process, and as a biographer of Wallenberg and Nobel I work in non-fiction. Both are context only and are not evidence of a preference for any candidate. Whether I vote is a modeling assumption and is not adjudicated here.
